lessons.title: Plants around us
objectives: Name some common garden and wild plants
Say the difference between a plant and an animal
Look carefully at a plant and describe it

keywords.def: a living thing that grows in soil and makes its own food
the part of a plant that is often colourful
a place where people grow plants
a plant that grows by itself without being planted

starter: Bismillah. Name two things that are alive.
What do animals need to stay alive?
Name one thing you can see in a garden.

teach.heading: What is a plant?
teach.note: Ask: 'Is a tree alive?' 'Can it run?' Establish plants are living but different from animals. Misconception: plants are not alive because they do not move.

teach.heading: Garden plants
bullets: Roses and daffodils are garden plants
Tomatoes and mint are garden plants
teach.note: Show clear photos. Ask 'Who plants these?' (people). Ask children what plants grow near their homes, including herbs and pot plants.

teach.heading: Wild plants
bullets: Daisies and dandelions are wild plants
Grass and moss are wild plants
teach.note: Show a daisy and a dandelion. Safe online task: children look from a window or garden. They must not pick or eat any wild plant, as some are harmful.

teach.heading: Looking closely
teach.note: Model a description: 'This leaf is green, long and thin.' Children describe a plant at home or a picture you show.

practice: Which is a garden plant: a rose or a dandelion growing in a crack?
Is a daisy alive? Tell your partner why.
Describe this picture of a leaf using colour, shape and size.
independent: Draw one garden plant and one wild plant. Label each with its name.
Write one sentence: 'A plant is a living thing because ...'
exit: Name one garden plant and one wild plant.
True or false: plants are alive.
lessons.homework: Draw a plant you can see at home or in a garden and write its name or colour.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a picture word bank (rose, daisy, grass, tree). Stretch: sort five plants into garden or wild and explain.

lessons.title: Parts of a plant
objectives: Name the roots, stem, leaf, flower and fruit
Say what each part does in simple words
Label a plant diagram

keywords.def: the part under the soil that takes in water
the part that holds the plant up and carries water
the flat part that helps the plant make food
a coloured part of a flower

starter: Bismillah. Name one garden plant and one wild plant.
Is a plant alive? How do you know?

teach.heading: Under the ground: roots
bullets: Roots hold the plant in place
teach.note: Show a picture of a pulled-up plant with roots visible. Ask 'Why does a plant need roots?' Compare to feet that keep us standing.

teach.heading: Stem and leaves
bullets: The stem holds the plant up
teach.note: Hold up a real stem (celery, or a stem of mint) if available. Keep language simple: leaves use sunlight to make food for the plant. Do not teach photosynthesis detail yet.

teach.heading: Flower and fruit
teach.note: Safe demo: cut open an apple at home or on video to show seeds. A grown-up should do the cutting. Ask 'What could grow from a seed?'

teach.heading: Allah made plants
teach.note: Link to gratitude. Gently mention Qur'an 6:99 (Allah sends down water from the sky and brings out plants) in simple words: 'Allah sends rain so plants can grow.'

practice: Which part of the plant is under the soil?
Match the part to the job: roots, stem, leaf. Jobs: takes in water, holds the plant up, helps make food.
Label the diagram of a flower plant: root, stem, leaf, flower.
independent: Draw a plant and label four parts: root, stem, leaf, flower.
Complete the sentences: 'The roots take in ...' and 'The stem holds ...'
exit: Which part takes in water: root or flower?
Name two parts of a plant.
lessons.homework: Find a plant at home and point to its leaf and stem. Tell a grown-up what each part does.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use colour-coded labels and a real plant on camera. Stretch: explain what would happen to a plant with no roots.

lessons.title: Deciduous and evergreen trees
objectives: Name the parts of a tree: trunk, branch, leaf, root
Know that deciduous trees lose their leaves in autumn
Know that evergreen trees keep green leaves all year

keywords.def: the thick main stem of a tree
a tree that loses its leaves in autumn
a tree that keeps green leaves all year
an arm of a tree that grows from the trunk

starter: Bismillah. Which part of a plant is under the soil?
Name the season when leaves fall off.

teach.heading: Parts of a tree
bullets: It has roots under the ground
teach.note: Show a labelled tree. Ask children to point to each part. A tree is a big plant with a woody trunk.

teach.heading: Deciduous trees
bullets: Oak and horse chestnut are deciduous
Their leaves change colour in autumn
teach.note: Show photos of an oak in summer and in autumn. Say 'deciduous' together slowly. Explain the tree rests in winter.

teach.heading: Evergreen trees
teach.note: Show a pine tree photo. Misconception: evergreens never lose any leaves; they do lose some, but never all at once.

teach.heading: Sorting trees
bullets: Look at the leaves in autumn
teach.note: Give a quick sorting game with six pictures. Children say 'deciduous' or 'evergreen'. Safe task: observe from a window; no climbing or touching unknown plants.

practice: Is an oak tree deciduous or evergreen?
A tree has green leaves in January. Which type is it?
Point to the trunk on this tree picture.
independent: Draw two trees side by side: one deciduous in autumn and one evergreen. Label each.
Write the words 'deciduous' and 'evergreen' and say what each means.
exit: Which tree loses its leaves in autumn?
lessons.homework: Look at trees on the way out or from a window. Tell a grown-up if each one has green leaves or not.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use matching cards with pictures and the two key words. Stretch: explain why an evergreen looks green in winter.

lessons.title: Autumn becomes winter
objectives: Name the four seasons in order
Describe changes in weather and daylight from autumn to winter
Say how animals and people get ready for winter

keywords.def: one of four parts of the year: spring, summer, autumn, winter
the time when it is light outside
to sleep through the winter
how hot or cold something is

starter: Bismillah. Name a tree that loses its leaves in autumn.
Is it hot or cold in winter?

teach.heading: Four seasons
bullets: They happen in the same order
teach.note: Use a cycle picture. Children say the seasons in order, with actions. Ask which season we are in now (November: autumn, nearly winter).

teach.heading: Weather changes
bullets: There is more rain and wind
teach.note: Ask children to look at today's weather. Compare to summer using pictures. Frost: tiny ice crystals on cold mornings.

teach.heading: Shorter days
teach.note: Safe demo: use a torch and a child's toy to show light. In November the sun sets early in the UK. Ask 'When did it get dark last night?'

teach.heading: Getting ready for winter
bullets: Birds may fly to warmer places
teach.note: Hedgehogs hibernate. Many birds migrate. Ask children how their family gets ready (coats, heating). Note Islamic ethos: thank Allah for warm homes and think of those who need help.

practice: Say the four seasons in order.
Which is more likely in winter: frost or a heatwave?
Why might a hedgehog hibernate in winter?
independent: Draw a picture of an autumn day and a winter day. Write one word for the weather on each.
Write two things that change from autumn to winter.
exit: Are days longer or shorter in winter?
lessons.homework: Look outside each morning this week and write or draw the weather. Is it getting colder?
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use a season picture strip with words; allow acting out. Stretch: explain why we cannot play outside as late in winter.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials (Moon Zoom! and Rain & Sunrays)
lessons.title: Object or material?
lessons.bigQuestion: What is a rocket made of?
objectives: To understand that every object is made from a material
successCriteria: All: name four materials: wood, plastic, glass, metal
Most: say what material an object is made from
Some: find one object made from two materials
lessons.crossCurricular: English: saying full sentences: 'It is made of ...'
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the materials Allah gave us

keywords.def: a thing you can see and touch
what a thing is made of
a material that comes from trees
a hard, shiny material, like a spoon
a material made in factories, used for bottles
a see-through material, used for windows

hook.text: A spoon and a fork are different objects. Can they be made of the same thing?

islamicLink.text: Allah made the world and everything in it. He made trees, rocks, water and metals for us to use. Allah says He sent down iron, which has many benefits for people (al-Hadid 57:25). We say alhamdulillah for the things we use every day.

starter.q: What do we call the big round thing in the night sky?
Name one thing in your bedroom.
starter.a: For example: a bed, a lamp, a book

teach.heading: Objects and materials
bullets: A material is what it is made of
A cup is an object; it can be glass or plastic
teach.note: Hold up a metal spoon. Say: this is an object. It is a spoon. It is made of metal. Metal is the material. Ask pupils to hold up one object near them.

teach.heading: Wood and metal
bullets: Metal is hard and often shiny
A rocket is made mostly of metal
teach.note: Show a wooden spoon and a metal spoon. Ask: how are they the same? How are they different? Rockets need strong metal to fly to space.

teach.heading: Plastic, glass, rock and water
teach.note: The Moon is made of rock. Astronauts brought Moon rock back to Earth. Water is a material too: it is in our cups and in the sea.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Give 30 seconds, then share the results.

check.q: A window is made of which material?
check.why: Windows are glass so we can see through them. Wood and rock are not see-through.

practice.q: What material is a metal spoon made of?
practice.model:
Look at the object.
It is a spoon.
It is hard and shiny.
It is made of metal.

practice.q: What material is a window made of?
What material is a pencil made of?

independent.q: Core: Material hunt. Find one object made of wood, metal, plastic and glass. Show each one to the camera.
independent.a: For example: wooden spoon, metal key, plastic bottle, glass jar
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: I found a jar. It is made of glass. I put it on the glass card.

independent.q: Extend: Find an object made of rock or stone.
independent.a: For example: a pebble or a stone step

independent.q: Stretch: Find one object made of two materials.
independent.a: For example: a pencil (wood and graphite) or a chair (wood and metal)

exit.q: A key is made of:
exit.a: B) metal

exit.q: Big question: what is a rocket made of?
exit.a: Mostly metal, because metal is strong

lessons.homework: Material hunt at home: find one object made of each of six materials (wood, plastic, glass, metal, water, rock) and tell an adult.
lessons.send: SEND: real objects to hold and picture cards of the six materials. EAL: say 'It is made of ...' with each object. Stretch: sort objects made of two materials.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials (Moon Zoom! and Rain & Sunrays)
lessons.title: Hard or soft, bendy or stiff?
lessons.bigQuestion: Which material would you choose for a window, and why?
objectives: To understand that materials have properties we can test by touch and sight
successCriteria: All: say if a material is hard or soft
Most: sort objects by one property
Some: say if a material is see-through or not
lessons.smsc: Moral: handling objects carefully and safely at home

keywords.def: what a material is like
does not squash when you press it
squashes when you press it
bends easily
you can see through it
you cannot see through it

hook.text: Why is a window not made of wood?

islamicLink.text: Allah made each material different. Some are hard like rock and some are soft like wool. Allah says He made for us from the wool of animals things we use and enjoy (an-Nahl 16:80). Choosing the right material is using Allah's gifts wisely.

starter.q: What material is a spoon often made of?
Name a material that comes from trees.
A bottle is often made of:

teach.heading: What is a property?
bullets: A property tells us what a material is like
teach.note: Press a sponge, then a stone. Ask: which squashed? The sponge is soft. The stone is hard. Hard and soft are properties.

teach.heading: Can we see through it?
bullets: Transparent: we can see through it
Opaque: we cannot see through it
Glass is transparent; wood is opaque
teach.note: Hold a glass jar and a wooden board in front of a toy. Ask: can you see the toy?

teach.heading: Sort them
bullets: Put each one in a group
teach.note: Pupils call out the letter and group. Bend gently; never bend glass.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results and ask one pupil why.

check.why: A cushion squashes when pressed. A brick and a pan are hard.

practice.q: Is a sponge hard or soft?
practice.model:
Press it.
It squashes.
So it is soft.

practice.q: Is a metal spoon bendy or stiff?
Can you see through cling film?

independent.q: Core: Find four objects at home. Show each one and say 'hard' or 'soft'.
independent.a: For example: book hard, sock soft, cup hard, towel soft
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: this is a towel. I press it. It squashes. It is soft.

independent.q: Extend: Which of your objects is bendy?
independent.a: For example: a sock, a plastic ruler, a rubber band

independent.q: Stretch: Why is a window made of glass and not wood?
independent.a: Glass is transparent, so light comes in and we can see out

exit.q: A window is:
exit.a: A) transparent

exit.q: Big question: which material would you choose for a window, and why?
exit.a: Glass, because it is transparent and hard

lessons.homework: Hold four objects up to a lamp or window with an adult: which ones let light through?
lessons.send: SEND: feel-and-say with a real sponge and stone; picture cards for hard and soft. EAL: hard, soft, bendy, see-through with actions. Stretch: describe one object with two properties.

Household items: sponge, stone, metal spoon, cushion, cling film, wooden block
Mini-whiteboard and pen

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials (Moon Zoom! and Rain & Sunrays)
lessons.title: Which fabric would make a good rain hat?
lessons.bigQuestion: How can we find out which fabric keeps rain out?
objectives: To understand how a simple test can show which material is waterproof
successCriteria: All: say what waterproof means
Most: predict which fabric will keep water out
Some: say how to keep the test fair
lessons.smsc: Social: working safely with an adult helper

keywords.def: does not let water through
soaks up water
a soft material made for clothes
a way to find something out
say what you think will happen

hook.text: Why do people wear a raincoat and not a towel when it rains?

islamicLink.text: Rain is a mercy from Allah. Allah says He sends down blessed rain from the sky and grows gardens with it (Qaf 50:9). We thank Allah for rain, and we choose clothes that keep us dry and warm.

starter.q: Is a sponge hard or soft?
Name one material that is opaque.

teach.heading: Waterproof or absorbent?
teach.note: Drip water on a plastic bag and on kitchen roll. Ask: what happened to the water on each?

teach.heading: Our test
bullets: Drip 5 spoons of water on top
teach.note: Model it slowly with an elastic band holding the fabric. Say: same cup, same water, same number of spoons for every fabric.

teach.heading: Keep it fair
teach.note: Ask: if I pour a jug on one and one spoon on another, is that fair? No.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results; ask why.

check.q: Which would make the best rain hat?
check.why: Plastic is waterproof. Kitchen roll and cotton soak up water.

practice.q: Predict: will water go through kitchen roll?
practice.model:
Kitchen roll soaks up water.
So water will go through.
I predict the cup will be wet.

practice.q: Predict: will water go through foil?
Why do we use 5 spoons of water every time?

independent.q: Core: With an adult, test three fabrics over a cup (a plastic bag, kitchen roll, an old sock). Put a tick if the cup stays dry.
independent.a: Plastic bag: tick (dry); kitchen roll: cross (wet); sock: cross (wet)
independent.model: Teacher shows it first with foil: foil on the cup, 5 spoons of water, wait, look. The cup is dry. Tick.

independent.q: Extend: Which fabric was best for a rain hat?
independent.a: The plastic bag, because it is waterproof

independent.q: Stretch: What one thing did you change in the test?
independent.a: Only the fabric

exit.q: Waterproof means:
exit.a: B) water does not go through

exit.q: Big question: how can we find out which fabric keeps rain out?
exit.a: Drip the same water on each fabric over a cup and see which cup stays dry

lessons.homework: Drip water on four household materials with an adult and record which let water through.
lessons.send: SEND: adult helper drips the water; tick or cross cards. EAL: wet, dry, waterproof with pictures. Stretch: test a fourth fabric and explain the result.

Results table: tick or cross for three fabrics (portal printable)
Three plastic cups, an elastic band, a teaspoon, water, a tray
Fabrics: a plastic bag (adult only, keep away from faces), kitchen roll, an old sock, foil

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Everyday materials (Moon Zoom! and Rain & Sunrays)
lessons.title: Winter weather and short days
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is it dark when we eat dinner in winter?
objectives: To understand that winter has cold weather and short days
successCriteria: All: name two kinds of winter weather
Most: say that winter days are short
Some: say that the sun sets a little later each day after winter starts
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: telling the time to the hour for sunset
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: noticing the signs of Allah in the seasons

keywords.def: the coldest season of the year
what it is like outside: sun, rain, wind
the time when the Sun lights the sky
when the Sun goes down
one of four parts of the year

hook.text: Is it light or dark when you wake up in January? What about July?

islamicLink.text: Allah made the seasons and the night and the day. Allah says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the changing of night and day there are signs for people who think (Al Imran 3:190). Short winter days remind us of Allah's perfect plan. We pray Maghrib after sunset, so in winter Maghrib comes early.

starter.q: Is a towel waterproof or absorbent?

teach.heading: The four seasons
bullets: January and February are in winter
Each season has its own weather
teach.note: Say the seasons in order together. Ask: which season are we in now?

teach.heading: Winter weather
bullets: We wear coats, hats and gloves
teach.note: Look out of the window together. Ask: what is the weather today? What are you wearing to go out?

teach.heading: Short days
bullets: In summer the Sun sets late
teach.note: In London in late December the Sun is up for about 8 hours. In June it is up for about 16 hours.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: Winter days are short. They are not always sunny: winter brings rain, wind and frost.

practice.q: Name two kinds of winter weather.
practice.a: For example: frost and rain, or snow and wind
practice.model:
Look outside.
It is cold.
There is frost on the grass.
Frost and wind are winter weather.

practice.q: Are winter days long or short?
What do we wear in winter to keep warm?
practice.a: For example: a coat, hat, gloves, scarf

independent.q: Core: Start your weather diary. Draw today's weather and write one word.
independent.a: For example: a cloud and the word 'cloudy'
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: I look out. It is grey and wet. I draw a cloud with rain. I write 'rainy'.

independent.q: Extend: Ask an adult what time the Sun will set today.
independent.a: About 4 to 5 o'clock in January and early February in the UK

independent.q: Stretch: Is the sunset earlier or later than last week?
independent.a: A little later, because the days are getting longer after winter begins

exit.q: January is in:
exit.a: A) winter

exit.q: Big question: why is it dark when we eat dinner in winter?
exit.a: Because winter days are short and the Sun sets early

lessons.homework: Record the weather and the sunset time each day for one week in your weather diary.
lessons.send: SEND: weather picture symbols to stick in the diary. EAL: sunny, rainy, windy, cold with pictures. Stretch: compare the sunset time on Monday and Friday.

Coloured pencils
A window to look out of (no going out alone)
Mini-whiteboard and pen

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The human body and senses (Memory Box and Human Senses)
lessons.title: Humans are mammals
lessons.bigQuestion: How are we like a cat, and how are we different?
objectives: To understand that humans are animals called mammals
successCriteria: All: name two animal groups
Most: say two things all mammals have
Some: say how a pet and a child are the same and different
lessons.crossCurricular: History: this week we also make our own timeline from baby to now
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the many animals Allah created

keywords.def: a person, like you and me
an animal with hair that feeds its babies milk
an animal that lives with us at home
an animal that lives in water and has fins
an animal with feathers and wings

hook.text: Is a person an animal? What makes you think so?

islamicLink.text: Allah created every living creature. Allah says that He created every animal from water (An-Nur 24:45). Some walk on two legs and some on four. People are special because Allah gave us minds to think.

starter.q: Wood, metal and glass are all ...

teach.heading: Animal groups
bullets: Each group has its own features
teach.note: Show each picture. Pupils say the group together. Fish have fins and scales; birds have feathers and wings.

teach.heading: What makes a mammal?
bullets: Hair or fur on the body
teach.note: Point to your own hair. We have hair, we breathe air and babies drink milk. So we are mammals too.

teach.heading: A pet and me
bullets: Different: we walk on two legs
teach.note: Compare a cat with a child. Ask: what is the same? What is different?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: A dog has fur and feeds its puppies milk. A goldfish is a fish; a robin is a bird.

practice.q: Is a human a mammal?
practice.model:
I look at me.
I have hair.
I breathe air.
I drank milk as a baby.
So I am a mammal.

practice.q: Name one thing all mammals have.
practice.a: Hair or fur (or: breathe air, drink milk as babies)

practice.q: A robin is a ...

independent.q: Core: Draw a pet or a farm animal and yourself. Circle one thing that is the same.
independent.a: For example: both have eyes, or both have hair
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: I draw a cat and me. Both of us have two eyes. I circle the eyes.

independent.q: Extend: Write one thing that is different.
independent.a: For example: a cat has a tail, I do not

independent.q: Stretch: Name a mammal that lives in the sea.
independent.a: A whale or a dolphin (or a seal)

exit.q: Humans are:
exit.a: Mammals

exit.q: Big question: how are we like a cat, and how are we different?
exit.a: Same: hair, eyes, breathe air, babies drink milk. Different: two legs, no tail, we talk

lessons.homework: Put five photos of yourself, from baby to now, in order and talk to your family about how you changed.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards for the sort; say the answer instead of writing. EAL: same and different with pictures. Stretch: sort five more animals into groups.

Animal picture cards for the sort, six cards (portal printable)
Paper and coloured pencils
Mini-whiteboard and pen

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The human body and senses (Memory Box and Human Senses)
lessons.title: Parts of the human body
lessons.bigQuestion: Which part of your body do you use the most?
objectives: To understand that the human body has parts with names and jobs
successCriteria: All: point to and name five body parts
Most: label a body outline
Some: say what one part helps us do
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: the body parts we wash in wudu
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: thanking Allah for a body that works

keywords.def: the top part of the body
joins the head to the body
where the arm joins the body
where the arm bends
where the leg bends
a word that names a part

hook.text: Can you touch your elbow with the same hand? Try it!

islamicLink.text: Allah says He created people in the best form (At-Tin 95:4). Every part of the body has a job. We use our hands, face and feet in wudu, and our knees and forehead in sujud.

starter.a: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds or mammals

teach.heading: Head to toe
teach.note: Do a spoken chant (no music): touch each part as we say it.

teach.heading: Bending parts
bullets: We can sit, kneel and pray
teach.note: Show bending the knees in sujud and sitting in salah. Our body helps us worship Allah.

teach.heading: How to label
bullets: Write the word at the end
teach.note: Model labelling the knee on a body outline with a ruler line.

steps: Find the knee on the picture
Draw a straight line from it

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: The elbow bends the arm; the knee bends the leg.

practice.q: Point to your shoulder. Show me!
practice.model:
I find my arm.
I follow it up to the top.
That is my shoulder.
I point to it.

practice.q: What joins your head to your body?
Which part bends your leg?

independent.q: Core: Label five parts on the body outline: head, neck, arm, knee, foot.
independent.a: Five correct labels with straight lines
independent.model: Teacher labels 'head' first: line from the head, write 'head'.

independent.q: Extend: Add elbow and shoulder.
independent.a: Two more correct labels

independent.q: Stretch: Write what your hands help you do.
independent.a: For example: hold a cup, write, make wudu

exit.q: The knee is on your:
exit.a: Leg

exit.q: Big question: which part of your body do you use the most?
exit.a: Any part with a reason, for example: my hands, to eat and write

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The human body and senses (Memory Box and Human Senses)
lessons.title: Sight and hearing
lessons.bigQuestion: Which would you find harder: a day with your eyes closed or with your ears covered?
objectives: To understand that we see with our eyes and hear with our ears
successCriteria: All: name the five senses
Most: match sight to eyes and hearing to ears
Some: say how we keep our eyes and ears safe
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: light from the Sun and lamps (Year 3 light)
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: gratitude for hearing and sight

keywords.def: the ways our body finds out about the world
seeing with our eyes
hearing sounds with our ears
the body part we see with
the body part we hear with

hook.text: Close your eyes and listen. What three sounds can you hear right now?

islamicLink.text: Allah brought us out of our mothers not knowing anything, and He gave us hearing, sight and hearts so that we may be grateful (An-Nahl 16:78). Our senses are a gift from Allah. We say alhamdulillah (الحمد لله) for them and use them for good.

starter.q: Humans are mammals. True or false?
Name one part of your leg.

teach.heading: Five senses
bullets: Each sense has a body part
teach.note: Count the five senses on one hand.

teach.heading: Sight
bullets: We cannot see in the dark
teach.note: Turn off a lamp in the room. Ask: can you see colours in the dark? We need light to see.

teach.heading: Hearing
bullets: We hear the adhan with our ears
teach.note: Make a quiet sound and a loud sound (tap, clap). Ask which was louder.

teach.heading: Keep them safe
bullets: Do not put things in ears
Keep screens a good distance away
teach.note: Explain each rule simply.

misconception.wrong: Sunglasses make it safe to look at the Sun
misconception.right: Never look straight at the Sun, even with sunglasses

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: Ears collect sounds. Eyes are for seeing.

practice.q: Which body part do we see with?
practice.model:
I close my eyes.
I cannot see.
I open them.
I can see.
So I see with my eyes.

practice.q: Clap quietly, then loudly. Which sense did you use?
How many senses do we have?

independent.q: Core: Look and listen. Draw one thing you can see and one thing you can hear at home.
independent.a: For example: see a clock; hear the kettle
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: I see a cup. I hear a car outside. I draw both.

independent.q: Extend: Write 'eyes' or 'ears' under each picture.
independent.a: Correct body part under each

independent.q: Stretch: Write one way to keep your ears safe.
independent.a: For example: do not put things in them; turn loud sounds down

exit.q: Sight goes with:
exit.a: Eyes

exit.q: Big question: which would be harder, eyes closed or ears covered?
exit.a: Any answer with a reason, for example: eyes closed, because I could not see where to walk

lessons.homework: Sit quietly for one minute at home and list the sounds you hear.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards of eyes and ears to hold up. EAL: see and hear with actions. Stretch: list three things that help blind or deaf people (white cane, hearing aid, sign language).

lessons.unit: Spring 2: The human body and senses (Memory Box and Human Senses)
lessons.title: Touch, taste and smell
lessons.bigQuestion: Could you find an orange with your eyes closed? How?
objectives: To understand that we touch with our skin, taste with our tongue and smell with our nose
successCriteria: All: name touch, taste and smell
Most: match each sense to its body part
Some: describe a smell or texture with a good word
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: recording results in a simple table
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: noticing the blessings of food and smells

keywords.def: feeling things with our skin
finding out flavours with our tongue
finding out about smells with our nose
covers our body and feels things
the body part we taste with
the body part we smell with

hook.text: What is your favourite smell? Is there a smell you do not like?

islamicLink.text: Allah brought us out of our mothers not knowing anything, and He gave us hearing, sight and hearts so that we may be grateful (An-Nahl 16:78). Our senses are a gift from Allah. We say alhamdulillah (الحمد لله) for them and use them for good.

starter.q: How many senses do we have?

teach.heading: Touch
teach.note: Feel a sponge and a spoon. Use the material words from Spring 1.

teach.heading: Taste and smell
teach.note: A lemon is sour. Honey is sweet. Only taste food an adult gives you.

teach.heading: Our sense test
teach.note: Safety first: only kitchen smells an adult chooses: lemon, cinnamon, mint. Waft, do not sniff hard. No tasting in this test.

steps: Waft the smell to my nose

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: The tongue tastes; the nose smells; the skin feels.

practice.q: Which body part feels a soft sponge?
practice.model:
I touch the sponge with my fingers.
Fingers have skin.
Skin feels soft and hard.
So touch uses skin.

practice.q: A lemon tastes:
Which sense tells you the bread is burning in the next room?

independent.q: Core: Do the smell test with three pots and record your guesses in the table.
independent.a: Three guesses recorded, for example lemon, cinnamon, mint
independent.model: Teacher shows pot 1 on camera: wafts, says 'fresh and sour', writes 'lemon'.

independent.q: Extend: Feely bag: touch two objects and say one word for each.
independent.a: For example: spoon smooth, sponge soft

independent.q: Stretch: Which sense is missing from our test?
independent.a: Taste (and sight, because our eyes were closed)

exit.q: Smell goes with:
exit.a: Nose

exit.q: Big question: could you find an orange with your eyes closed? How?
exit.a: Yes: smell it, feel its bumpy skin, or taste it

lessons.homework: Smell test at home: an adult chooses three kitchen smells; identify them with eyes closed and record your results.
lessons.send: SEND: real objects with picture labels; adult reads the table. EAL: smell, touch, taste with actions. Stretch: describe each smell with a new word. Allergy check before the lesson; nothing is eaten.

lessons.unit: Summer 1: Plants in spring and building materials (Bright Lights, Big City and How Do Leaves Change?)
lessons.title: Leaves and trees in spring
lessons.bigQuestion: What does a tree do in spring that it did not do in winter?
objectives: To understand how trees change in spring
successCriteria: All: name the parts of a tree
Most: say what buds and blossom are
Some: sort trees into deciduous and evergreen
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: noticing seasons where we live
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at how plants grow again each spring

keywords.def: a small bump that opens into a leaf or flower
flowers on a tree in spring
a tree that loses its leaves in autumn
a tree that keeps its leaves all year
the thick main stem of a tree

hook.text: Look out of the window. What has changed on the trees since winter?

islamicLink.text: Allah sends down rain from the sky, and by it He brings out plants of every kind (Al-An'am 6:99). Each spring the buds open again by His permission.

starter.q: Name one part of a plant.
starter.a: For example: root, stem, leaf or flower

teach.heading: Parts of a tree
bullets: Roots hold it in the ground
teach.note: Recap from autumn: a tree is a big plant.

teach.heading: Spring changes
bullets: New leaves are small and light green
teach.note: Show a bud, then blossom, then new leaves on a cherry or apple tree.

teach.heading: Two kinds of tree
bullets: Deciduous trees lose leaves in autumn
They grow new leaves in spring
Evergreen trees keep leaves all year
teach.note: Oak and horse chestnut are deciduous. Holly and pine are evergreen.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: A tree that keeps its leaves all year is:
check.why: Evergreen means always green; deciduous trees lose their leaves.

practice.q: What opens into a leaf in spring?
practice.model:
It is small and tight.
In spring it opens.
A leaf comes out.
It is a bud.

practice.q: Is an oak deciduous or evergreen?
What colour are new spring leaves?

independent.q: Core: Label the tree picture: roots, trunk, branches, leaves, blossom.
independent.a: Five correct labels
independent.model: Teacher labels 'trunk' first with a straight line.

independent.q: Extend: Draw one leaf you can see today.
independent.a: A careful leaf drawing

independent.q: Stretch: Why do new leaves grow in spring?
independent.a: It is warmer and lighter, so the tree can grow

exit.q: Blossom is:
exit.a: Flowers on a tree

exit.q: Big question: what does a tree do in spring?
exit.a: Its buds open, blossom comes out and new leaves grow

lessons.homework: Choose a tree near home. Draw it and one leaf now; we will compare it in the summer.
lessons.send: SEND: label stickers to place. EAL: tree word cards with pictures. Stretch: find a tree with blossom and name it.

lessons.unit: Summer 1: Plants in spring and building materials (Bright Lights, Big City and How Do Leaves Change?)
lessons.title: Why did London burn? Wood, brick and stone
lessons.bigQuestion: Which material would you choose to build a house that will not burn?
objectives: To understand why brick and stone are better than wood for building houses close together
successCriteria: All: name wood, brick and stone
Most: say which material burns
Some: explain why London was rebuilt in brick
lessons.crossCurricular: History: why London was rebuilt after the Great Fire
lessons.smsc: Moral: keeping our homes and neighbours safe

keywords.def: what something is made of
a material from trees; it can burn
a hard block made from baked clay
hard rock dug from the ground
right for the job

hook.text: Why do you think we do not build houses from paper?

starter.q: The Great Fire started in a:
A tree that loses its leaves is:
Name one thing that helped the fire spread.
starter.a: Wind, dry weather or wooden houses

teach.heading: Three building materials
bullets: Stone is dug from the ground
teach.note: Hold up a piece of wood, a brick (or photo) and a stone.

teach.heading: What are they like?
bullets: All three can be hard and strong
Brick and stone do not burn
teach.note: We do NOT test fire at home. We know this from scientists and from 1666.

teach.heading: After the fire
bullets: Houses had to be brick or stone
teach.note: This is why old London streets have brick houses.

teach.heading: Our safe test
bullets: Scratch with a coin: does it mark?
Drip water: does it soak in?
teach.note: With an adult only. No fire, no flames. Use a wooden spoon, a stone and a brick or tile.

model.problem: Scratch test on the wooden spoon

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: Brick is baked clay and does not burn; wood and paper both burn.

practice.q: Is wood or brick better for houses close together?
practice.model:
Houses close together can catch fire from each other.
Wood burns.
Brick does not burn.
So brick is better.

practice.q: What is brick made from?

independent.q: Core: Do the scratch and water tests on wood and stone (and brick if you have one) and tick the table.
independent.a: Wood marks and soaks up some water; stone is hard to mark; results recorded
independent.model: Teacher does the wooden spoon scratch test on camera first.

independent.q: Extend: Write which material you would build with and why.
independent.a: For example: brick, because it is strong and does not burn

independent.q: Stretch: What else is made of wood in your home?
independent.a: For example: a door, a table, a spoon

exit.q: After 1666, new houses were built of:
exit.a: Brick or stone

exit.q: Big question: which material would you choose and why?
exit.a: Brick or stone, because they are strong and do not burn

lessons.homework: Find three things at home made of wood and three made of stone or brick; tell an adult.
lessons.send: SEND: picture table to tick. EAL: wood, brick, stone with real objects. Stretch: why might stone be harder to build with than wood?

lessons.title: The four seasons
lessons.bigQuestion: Why does the same tree look so different in winter and in summer?
objectives: To understand that the year has four seasons, each with its own weather and changes
successCriteria: All: name the four seasons in order
Most: say what the weather is like in summer
Some: spot one summer change in plants or animals
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the weather chart we start in our next lesson
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at how the seasons change each year

keywords.def: one of the four parts of the year
the season when plants start to grow and buds open
the warmest season, with long sunny days
the season when leaves change colour and fall
the coldest season, with short days

hook.text: What is your favourite season, and what can you see, hear and feel in it?

islamicLink.text: Allah made the sun a shining light and the moon a light, so that we can count the years and keep track of time (Yunus 10:5). The seasons come round every year, just as Allah made them.

starter.q: A tree that loses its leaves is:
Name one material that does not burn easily.

teach.heading: Four seasons
teach.note: Say the order together, pointing round the circle. The seasons go round like a wheel.

teach.heading: Weather in each season
teach.note: These are what is usual in the UK. Some summer days are rainy too.

teach.heading: Summer changes now
teach.note: Look at the photo of a tree in summer. Compare it with the same kind of tree in winter.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: The order is spring, summer, autumn, winter. Autumn follows summer.

practice.q: Which season comes after winter?
practice.model:
I say the order: spring, summer, autumn, winter.
After winter we start again.
So spring comes after winter.

practice.q: Which season is the warmest?
In which season do leaves fall?

independent.q: Core: Draw a tree in summer and a tree in winter, side by side. Write the season under each.
independent.a: Summer: green leaves; winter: bare branches
independent.model: Teacher draws the trunk of the summer tree first and adds leaves.

independent.q: Extend: Write one weather word for summer and one for winter.
independent.a: For example: sunny; frosty

independent.q: Stretch: Why do we wear different clothes in summer and winter?
independent.a: Summer is warm so we wear light clothes; winter is cold so we wear warm coats

exit.q: The coldest season is:
exit.a: Winter

exit.q: Big question: why does a tree look different in winter and summer?
exit.a: In winter it has no leaves; in summer it has green leaves because it is warm and sunny

lessons.homework: Look out of the window each day this week and say which season it is and one thing that tells you.
lessons.send: SEND: four season picture cards to order. EAL: season words with pictures. Stretch: say how animals change in winter.

Pencil and coloured pencils

lessons.title: Day length through the year
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can you still play outside at bedtime in June but not in December?
objectives: To understand that day length changes with the seasons
successCriteria: All: say that summer days are longer than winter days
Most: use the words sunrise and sunset
Some: compare a summer and a winter sunset time
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading a bar chart and telling the time to the hour
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at night and day following each other

keywords.def: how long it is light from sunrise to sunset
when the sun comes up in the morning
when the sun goes down in the evening
more time
less time

hook.text: In which season does the sun stay up longest? How could you check?

islamicLink.text: Allah tells us that in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the changing of night and day there are signs for people who think (Al Imran 3:190). The days grow long and short again, just as Allah made them.

teach.heading: Sunrise and sunset
teach.note: Never look straight at the sun. We notice the sky getting light and dark.

teach.heading: Long summer days
bullets: In June the sun sets about 9 pm
About 16 hours of daylight in London
The longest day is near 21 June
teach.note: Times are for London and rounded. Ask: what are you doing at 9 pm?

teach.heading: Short winter days
bullets: In December the sun sets before 4 pm
The shortest day is near 21 December
teach.note: Compare with the winter sunset times pupils recorded in their weather diary in Spring 1.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: Which month has the longest days?
check.why: Summer days are longest; the longest day is near 21 June.

practice.q: Read the chart: how many hours of daylight in June?
practice.model:
I find June on the chart.
I look at the top of its bar.
It reaches 16, so about 16 hours.

practice.q: Which month on the chart has the shortest days?
Is a summer day longer or shorter than a winter day?

independent.q: Core: Fill in the sentence: In summer the days are ___ and in winter the days are ___.
independent.a: Longer; shorter
independent.model: Teacher fills in a first sentence about light: 'In summer it is light at bedtime.'

independent.q: Extend: Draw the sky at 8 pm in June and at 8 pm in December.
independent.a: June: light sky with sun low; December: dark sky with moon or stars

independent.q: Stretch: How many more hours of daylight does June have than December?
independent.a: About 8 more hours (16 take away 8)

exit.q: Sunset is when the sun:
exit.a: Goes down

exit.q: Big question: why can you play outside at bedtime in June?
exit.a: Summer days are long, so it is still light in the evening

lessons.homework: With an adult, check what time the sun sets tonight and compare it with your winter sunset record.
lessons.send: SEND: sun-up and sun-down picture cards. EAL: sunrise, sunset, longer, shorter with pictures. Stretch: find out the time of sunrise tomorrow.
